notes.meaning: God tells Ezekiel to sing a lament, a sad song like the ones sung at a funeral. It is for the last kings of Judah, the sons and grandsons of good King Josiah. The people often complained about their troubles but never asked why they came. This song from God shows the real cause.

The "mother" is the nation of Judah and its city Jerusalem, which gave birth to its kings. She is pictured as a fierce lioness. She lay down among lions, meaning she mixed with the cruel kings of the nations around her and copied their ways. God had called his people to be different from the nations. Instead, she raised her royal sons to act like those nations.

The first young lion is King Jehoahaz, a son of Josiah. Once he was king, he quickly showed a cruel side. He treated his own people like prey and took what they had. It is sad because his father Josiah had been one of Judah's most godly kings.

The nations heard about him. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, captured Jehoahaz and took him away to Egypt. The "pit" is a picture of a hidden trap dug to catch wild animals. The "hooks" were put in the noses of captured beasts and sometimes of captives. Jehoahaz was never heard of again.

The nation waited for Jehoahaz to come back from Egypt, but that hope came to nothing. So another son of Josiah, Jehoiakim, was made king. The people had been punished but had not changed their hearts.

Jehoiakim did not learn from his brother's fate. He copied the cruel kings around him and made friends with them. He took his people's money and land by unfair means. He ruled about eleven years and led Judah into worshiping idols.

His cruelty brought ruin to buildings and cities across the land. Older translations put the first line differently, but they agree on the main point. He was like a lion whose roar alone makes every animal shake. His threats frightened the people so much that towns and villages were left empty.

Then the nations came against him from every side. They were the Babylonians along with bands of Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites (2 Kings 24:2). Spreading a net is a picture of their plans and plots to catch him. Like a hunted lion, he was trapped.

He was bound in chains and brought to the king of Babylon. His roar was no longer heard on Israel's mountains, which means his bullying rule was over. God is fair when those who terrified others end up caught and afraid themselves.

Now the song uses a new picture. The mother, the nation, was like a healthy vine planted by water. This is the rich, well-watered land of Canaan God gave his people from their very beginning. Older translations read "in thy blood" here, but some scholars think the words meant "in your vineyard."

The vine's strong branches stand for the kings who came from David's family, like rods fit to be a ruler's scepter. Its great height shows how strong, rich and many the people once were. Remembering this past glory was meant to help them see how far they had fallen because of sin.

The vine was suddenly pulled up in anger. God used the king of Babylon to do it, and the "east wind" pictures the Babylonians. It did not slowly wither, and that suddenness showed it was God's hand, not chance. The strong branches were broken and burned. Zedekiah's sons were killed, and he was taken to Babylon in chains.

The vine is now planted in a dry desert. This is the people's exile, when they were carried off to Babylon. Babylon was really a fertile land, but to captives it felt like a wilderness. Even so, there is mercy here: God kept a small part of the vine alive, and later his people returned home.

The fire came from one of the vine's own branches. King Zedekiah broke his promise to Babylon and rebelled, which brought ruin on the whole nation. So the disaster was their own fault, not only Babylon's, and no king from David's line was left to rule. Christian readers see hope here in Jesus, the true Vine and promised Branch from David's family. The song was sad when it was given, and it would be sung as a lament for generations.
